items.prompt: What is a flaky test?
choices: One that gives different results on the same code
One that fails on every single run of the suite, always
One that has no checks inside it at all
items.explanation: Flakiness means unstable outcomes with no relevant change in the code or the test.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, which run order makes test B fail?
choices: Test B first, then test A
Test A first, then test B
Neither order makes it fail
items.explanation: A leaves an item in the shared list, so B no longer sees an empty list.

items.prompt: Between a passing and a failing run in the Scenario, what changed?
choices: The code inside test B was edited between runs
The code inside test A
Only the order the tests ran in
items.explanation: Code and tests were identical; the order was the only difference.

items.prompt: Is test B's check (the list starts empty) wrong?
choices: No, it is reasonable on its own
Yes, it should expect one item
Yes, it should check nothing
items.explanation: The check is fine. The test just depends on state it does not control.

items.prompt: What does test isolation mean?
choices: Every single test runs on its own separate computer
A test's result does not depend on other tests
A test runs only once ever
items.explanation: Isolated tests produce the same result in any order and alongside any other test.

items.prompt: What is environment leakage?
choices: A test printing far too much text to the build log
A test running slowly on CI
Leftover state from one test affecting another
items.explanation: State created by one test and not cleaned up leaks into later tests.

items.prompt: What leaked between the two tests in the Scenario?
choices: Test A's order stayed in the shared list
Test B's name stayed in memory
The CI machine's clock setting
items.explanation: The shared list kept the item A added, and B then saw it.

items.prompt: Re-running the same failed commit turns it green. What does that most suggest?
choices: The code is now definitely correct and final
The result varies without any code change
CI has fixed the test file itself
items.explanation: Same commit, different result: that is the signature of non-determinism.

items.prompt: A test fails on 1 of every 20 runs of an unchanged commit. How should it be classified?
choices: Broken: any failure at all means broken code
Flaky: it varies while the code stays the same
Fine: 19 passes out of 20 is a pass overall
Slow: the failures come from time limits only
items.explanation: Unstable results on unchanged code define flakiness; the occasional pass does not make it healthy.
items.reference:
Flaky versus broken
🔁 flaky: same code, different results
🧱 broken: same code, same failure every time
🧪 the assertion is usually fine
🎲 the result leans on something uncontrolled
Why: a flaky test is defined by unstable results on unchanged code, not by a wrong check.
items.learnMore:
Unstable result, stable code

The signal for flakiness is that nothing relevant changed between a pass and a fail. If the code under test changed, a new failure is information, not flakiness.

Common mistake

Assuming a test that fails now and then must contain a wrong assertion.
items.reflection: Think of an appliance or app that only misbehaves sometimes. What might it secretly depend on that you never see?

items.prompt: A test starts failing on every run right after someone edited the function it checks. Which statement fits?
choices: Not flaky; the change is the likely cause
Flaky, because the failure started suddenly
Flaky, because tests fail for random reasons
Not flaky, because only the test file is guilty
items.explanation: A consistent failure after a relevant change is ordinary breakage, not instability on unchanged code.

choices: A longer timeout so that slow runs can still finish
A random seed so the order is reshuffled
An assertion that expects one pending item
Isolation from state other tests leave behind
items.explanation: B's outcome depends on A having run, which is exactly what isolation rules out.

choices: The test fails identically in every order
The test fails only on the last weekend of each year
The test passes when run alone and fails after others
The test fails only when the browser window is narrow
items.explanation: Passing alone but failing after other tests means state left behind by them is changing the outcome.

items.prompt: Why can a laptop run stay green while CI goes red?
choices: CI always contains extra bugs that no laptop ever has
Laptops skip every test that could fail
CI reaches execution orders the laptop never uses
items.explanation: The bug exists in both places; only CI creates the triggering condition.

items.prompt: Which of these is typical of CI but not of one developer's laptop?
choices: Parallel workers and shuffled order
Using a different programming language
Reading the test files from disk
items.explanation: Parallelism and shuffling vary the conditions each run.

items.prompt: On a laptop that runs tests in one fixed order every time, what happens to an order bug?
choices: It triggers on every single run that happens
It may never trigger, so it stays hidden
It is removed by the operating system
items.explanation: With only one order ever sampled, a bad order is never reached.

items.prompt: Is CI the source of the shared-list bug?
choices: Yes, CI quietly adds the shared list on its own
Yes, CI rewrites the tests when it runs
No, it only exposes a bug already present
items.explanation: The shared list is in the code; CI merely runs a different order.

items.prompt: If a suite passes locally, what can you conclude?
choices: It passes under the conditions your laptop tried
It will pass under every condition that CI could try
It contains no shared state at all
items.explanation: A local pass is a narrow sample, not a proof about every condition.

items.prompt: Which run setup is most likely to expose an order-dependent bug?
choices: The same fixed order repeated another ten times
Randomized test order across several workers
One test run alone every time
items.explanation: Only varying the order can hit the bad one.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'CI is just flaky'. What is the better question?
choices: Why is CI so unreliable on this branch today?
Can we disable CI for this branch?
What does the failing test depend on?
items.explanation: The useful move is finding the uncontrolled dependency the CI conditions exposed.

items.prompt: How many orders does a laptop that always runs A then B ever try?
choices: One
Two
None
items.explanation: It runs exactly one fixed order, so the other order is never exercised.

items.prompt: The same 40 tests run in a fixed order on a laptop and in shuffled order on CI. A shared-state bug exists. What is the most likely result?
choices: Both fail on every single run because the bug exists
Laptop stays green; CI fails when a bad order occurs
Laptop fails more often since it has less memory
Both stay green since the bug is in the test only
items.explanation: A fixed order may never hit the bad sequence, while shuffling eventually does.
items.reference:
Narrow sample versus wide sample
💻 laptop: one machine, one fixed order
🤖 CI: shuffled order, parallel workers, busy hosts
🕳️ a bug needs its trigger condition to appear
🔍 the wider sample hits more conditions
Why: CI does not create the bug; it reaches conditions the laptop never reaches.
items.learnMore:
Where the bug lived all along

A dependency on order or timing exists on every machine. Whether it shows depends on whether the run happens to create the condition that triggers it.

Common mistake

Treating a CI-only failure as noise because it never reproduces on a laptop.
items.reflection: Where in your life does something work fine in your usual routine but break when conditions shift (a different route, a different time)?

items.prompt: A team merges whenever the local run is green and treats CI failures as noise. What is the flaw?
choices: A local run is a narrow sample of conditions
CI runs are always slower and less accurate
Local runs skip the assertions in every test
CI failures are always caused by the CI vendor
items.explanation: Ignoring CI failures lets order and timing dependencies ship and resurface later.

Delete the tests that failed in the last run
Run only the changed test files in isolation
Run the suite in random order a few times
items.explanation: Varying the order samples the conditions the bug needs; repeating one order cannot.

A syntax error present only in one of the files
B,A exposes state the tests share through a leak
A timeout setting that is too low for both tests
items.explanation: Order-specific failure of otherwise passing tests points to leftover shared state.

items.prompt: A test uses Math.random() with no fixed value. Which cause is this?
choices: Shared state
Real randomness
Unfinished async work
items.explanation: A new random value each run is uncontrolled input.

items.prompt: A test checks a result before the background task is done. Which cause?
choices: Real randomness
Real time
Unfinished async work
items.explanation: The check races the operation it depends on.

items.prompt: A test reads the system clock to pick a label. Which cause?
choices: Real time
Shared state
Real randomness
items.explanation: The result depends on when the test runs.

items.prompt: Two tests write to one shared file. Which cause?
choices: Real time
Shared state
Unfinished async work
items.explanation: The outcome depends on what the other test left in the file.

items.prompt: What is the usual fix for shared state?
choices: Add a longer delay between all the tests
Run the tests more times
Give each test fresh state of its own
items.explanation: Fresh state removes the shared object.

items.prompt: What is the usual fix for real time?
choices: Pass in or freeze the time
Run the test at a quiet hour
Update the expected value daily
items.explanation: A controlled time makes expected and actual agree always.

items.prompt: What is the usual fix for unfinished async work?
choices: Check twice and keep the second result
Wait for the operation being asserted
Skip the check on slow machines
items.explanation: Waiting for the exact operation removes the race.

items.prompt: Are the four causes unavoidable risks of testing?
choices: Yes, every suite will always flake
Yes, but only on CI machines
No, each has a deterministic fix
items.explanation: Flakiness marks an uncontrolled dependency, not an inherent cost.

items.prompt: A test builds an invoice id from a random generator, then compares it to a hardcoded id. Which fix removes the flake?
choices: Run the test several times and keep the best run
Inject the id or seed the generator
Extend the timeout for slower machines
Give each test its own empty list first
items.explanation: The expected id must be fixed; seeding or injecting makes the value predictable.
items.reference:
Four hidden dependencies
📒 shared state: result depends on who ran first
🕒 real time: clock or fixed delays
🎲 real randomness: new value every run
⏳ unfinished async: check runs too early
Why: each cause is an input the test never pinned down, so each has a deterministic fix.
items.learnMore:
Pin the input down

Every cause is a missing control: fresh state, a supplied time, a seeded or injected value, a wait on the exact operation. Once the input is fixed, the result is fixed.

Common mistake

Believing flakiness is unavoidable when testing async or stateful code.
items.reflection: Pick a process you rely on (a commute, a recipe). Which of the four kinds of uncontrolled input would break it most often?

items.prompt: A check on a 'processed' flag passes on fast machines and fails on busy ones. Which cause and fix pair is right?
choices: Unfinished async work; wait on the operation
Real time; freeze the clock throughout the test run
Shared state; create a new store per test
Real randomness; seed the generator first
items.explanation: The check races a background operation, so the fix is waiting for that operation itself.

items.prompt: A test fails 5% of the time per run. What is the chance it fails on a single run?
items.explanation: The per-run rate is the chance for one run.

items.prompt: What is the chance a 5% flake passes on one run?
items.explanation: Passing is the complement of failing: 100% minus 5%.

items.prompt: As the number of runs grows, the chance of at least one failure...
choices: Stays exactly the same
Shrinks toward zero
Grows toward certainty
items.explanation: More chances to fail means a higher chance of seeing one.

items.prompt: Does the chance of seeing a flake in 20 runs exceed the chance in 1 run?
choices: Yes, it is much larger
No, the two chances are exactly equal
No, it is smaller
items.explanation: 20 runs give about 64.2% against 5% for one.

items.prompt: Which number is the chance of at least one failure in 20 runs at 5%?
choices: About 12.5%
About 64.2%
About 35.8%
items.explanation: 1 minus 0.95 to the 20th power is about 0.642.

items.prompt: What does the 'at least one failure' calculation assume?
choices: Every run takes exactly the same time
CI uses a fixed order
Runs are independent of each other
items.explanation: The formula treats each run's failure as an independent chance.

items.prompt: What is the chance of a 5% flake failing at least once in 1 run?
items.explanation: With one run the formula reduces to the per-run rate.

items.prompt: A 50% flake is run twice. Is at least one failure more or less likely than 50%?
choices: Less likely
More likely
Exactly 50%
items.explanation: It is 75%: two chances beat one.

items.prompt: A test fails 5% of runs. About how likely is at least one failure in 10 independent runs?
choices: About 50.0%
About 40.1%
About 59.9%
About 5.0%
items.explanation: 1 minus 0.95 to the 10th is about 0.401; the naive 50% sum overcounts.
items.reference:
Chance of at least one failure
1️⃣ chance a run passes: 1 minus the flake rate
✖️ n runs pass: multiply that n times
➖ at least one failure: 1 minus that product
📈 climbs fast as runs pile up
Why: a small per-run chance repeated across many runs becomes a large chance of seeing it.
items.learnMore:
Small times many is big

A 5% flake looks harmless once. Across 20 runs the chance of at least one failure is about 64.2%, assuming independent runs.

Common mistake

Adding the per-run chances (10 runs at 5% is not 50%).
items.reflection: Think of a small risk you accept once (a rare mistake). What happens to your odds if you repeat it daily for a month?

items.prompt: A test fails half of all runs. What is the chance of at least one failure in 2 independent runs?
items.explanation: The chance both pass is 0.5 times 0.5, which is 25%, so one or more fail 75%.

choices: Each run's chance of failing falls as more runs happen in total
The first run counts differently from the rest
CI hides the rest of the failures after one
Failures in different runs can overlap, so chances do not just add
items.explanation: The correct value is about 40.1%; simple addition double counts overlapping outcomes.

items.prompt: Rerunning a red build until it turns green...
choices: Fixes the cause of the failure for good
Proves the test is correct
Hides the failure but leaves the cause
items.explanation: The dependency remains and will fail again.

items.prompt: Adding a longer fixed delay before a check...
choices: Shrinks the timing window but not removes it
Removes the race entirely and for good, always
Makes the test run faster
items.explanation: A window still exists; it is just smaller.

items.prompt: Which fix removes shared state for good?
choices: A reset line placed in one test only
Fresh state built for each test
Running that test first
items.explanation: No shared object means nothing to leak.

items.prompt: Why is a reset line in one test a weaker fix?
choices: It makes the whole test suite slower by an hour
It changes the assertion's meaning
Every other test must also remember to reset
items.explanation: Correctness then depends on every author remembering.

items.prompt: A flaky test usually passes. Is it fine to leave it?
choices: No, it still hides a real dependency
Yes, usually passing means it is correct
Yes, flakes never matter
items.explanation: A 1 in 20 failure still means an uncontrolled input.

items.prompt: Which approach treats the symptom?
choices: Inject the time into the function
Rerun the job until it passes
Await the operation being checked
items.explanation: The other two remove a cause.

items.prompt: Which approach treats the cause?
choices: Add a longer sleep before every check
Rerun the build
Await the operation being asserted
items.explanation: Awaiting the operation removes the race.

items.prompt: If one test shares state, what about others using the same helper?
choices: They are likely to flake too
They are guaranteed to be safe
They cannot run in CI
items.explanation: The pattern is shared, so the risk is shared.

items.prompt: A race flake is 'fixed' by doubling a fixed wait from 10 ms to 20 ms. What is the best description?
choices: The race is gone since the wait doubled
The window shrank, but a race still exists
The race got worse since waits are slower
The race is gone because the test is slower
items.explanation: A fixed wait only makes the bad timing rarer; waiting on the operation removes it.
items.reference:
Hide versus remove
🔁 rerun until green: hides one failure
⏲️ longer delay: shrinks the window only
🧹 reset in one test: others can forget
✅ fresh state per test: nothing left to forget
Why: a fix is only real when the uncontrolled dependency is gone, not merely rarer.
items.learnMore:
Rarer is not fixed

A longer wait or a rerun lowers the chance you see the failure but leaves the cause. Removal means the dependency no longer exists.

Common mistake

Counting a lowered failure rate as a solved problem.
items.reflection: Recall a problem you 'fixed' by working around it. Did the cause disappear, or only the symptom for a while?

items.explanation: The shared object still exists, so any test that forgets to reset reintroduces the bug.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a weak fix with the stronger replacement?
choices: Rerun until green; a longer sleep
Reset in one test; run that test first
Longer sleep; await the exact operation
Fixed clock; read the real time instead
items.explanation: Waiting on the operation removes the race; the other pairs swap strong for weak or are backwards.

Common mistake

Counting a lowered failure rate as a solved problem.

items.prompt: What is wrong with checking the status on the line right after starting the work?
choices: The work may not have finished yet
The status can never be read
The work finishes before it starts
items.explanation: The check races the operation.

items.prompt: What does await do with a promise?
choices: Cancels the promise
Waits until the promise resolves
Repeats the promise twice
items.explanation: Code after the await runs once the operation finishes.

items.prompt: In the diagram, when does the status get set?
choices: Before the test even starts running at all
Never
Later, after the test's immediate check
items.explanation: The background work finishes after the early check ran.

items.prompt: Which fix removes the race?
choices: Await the operation, then check
Check twice quickly
Rename the status field
items.explanation: Awaiting guarantees ordering.

items.prompt: Why does the early check mostly fail and sometimes pass?
choices: It depends on the test's name
It depends on timing luck
It depends on the file size
items.explanation: Only a stall could let the work finish first.

items.prompt: Is a longer fixed sleep a real fix?
choices: Yes, it removes the race
Yes, it speeds up the test
No, it only narrows the window
items.explanation: A guessed sleep can still be too short.

items.prompt: What should a test wait for before asserting on async work?
choices: The exact operation being asserted
A random number of milliseconds
The next test to start
items.explanation: Wait for the operation, not for time.

items.prompt: If a function returns a promise and you ignore it, the check runs...
choices: After the operation, always
Without waiting for the operation
Never
items.explanation: Ignoring the promise skips the wait.

items.prompt: A test starts a 10 ms operation, then checks the result immediately. Which description is right?
choices: It passes always, since 10 ms is very short
It races the operation and passes only by luck
It fails always, since the status is never set
It passes always, since the check comes second
items.explanation: The check runs before the timer callback, so the result depends on timing.
items.reference:
Check after the work finishes
▶️ start the operation
⏳ wait for that same operation to complete
✅ then check the result
🚫 a bigger fixed sleep still guesses
Why: waiting on the operation itself guarantees the result exists before the check.
items.learnMore:
Wait for the thing, not for time

Awaiting the returned promise ties the check to the operation finishing. Sleeping for a guessed duration ties it to a clock and keeps a window open.

Common mistake

Forgetting that a function returning a promise must be awaited before asserting.
items.reflection: When you wait for a delivery, do you wait a guessed number of hours or until the confirmation arrives? Where else do you guess instead of waiting for the signal?

items.prompt: Implement isExpired(createdAt, now, limit): true only when the age (now minus createdAt) is greater than limit. Times are plain numbers of minutes.
items.explanation: The function compares two numbers it is given, so it needs no clock. Greater-than (not greater-or-equal) makes exactly 30 not expired.

items.prompt: Implement minutesSince(then, now) returning how many minutes passed. Times are plain numbers of minutes.
items.explanation: Subtracting the supplied start from the supplied now gives a result that depends only on the arguments.

items.prompt: Implement isDiscountDay(dayOfWeek): true only on day 1 (Monday). The day is passed in as a number from 0 to 6.
items.explanation: Receiving the day removes the dependence on the date the test happens to run.

items.prompt: Implement isSessionActive(startedAt, now, ttl): true while the age is less than ttl (strictly). Times are plain numbers.
items.explanation: Strict less-than makes the boundary age (exactly ttl) inactive; both timestamps come from the arguments.

items.prompt: Implement isFuture(timestamp, now): true when timestamp is later than now. Times are plain numbers.
items.explanation: Comparing against the supplied now keeps the check pure.

items.prompt: Implement ageLabel(createdAt, now): return "fresh" if the age is under 10, "stale" if it is 10 up to and including 30, and "expired" if it is over 30. Times are plain numbers of minutes.
items.explanation: Computing the age once from the arguments makes both boundaries (10 and 30) checkable exactly. Order of the branches keeps each range exclusive of the next.
items.reference:
Supply the time
🕒 real clock: different every run
📥 pass the current time in as an argument
🔢 the test chooses both timestamps
📏 boundary cases become one-line checks
Why: a function that receives the time is a pure comparison, so its result never depends on when it runs.
items.learnMore:
Time as an input

Reading the clock inside the function hides an input. Making it a parameter exposes it so the test can pick any moment, including the exact boundary.

Common mistake

Hardcoding an expected value tied to today's date.
items.reflection: Where do you rely on 'now' in a decision (deadlines, expiry)? What would you check if you could set the clock yourself?

items.explanation: Strictly less than the cooldown means waiting; reaching exactly the cooldown flips to ready. No clock is read.
